title: Yennecock / Southold Town
summary: Yennicock and Yennicott are spellings preserved for the North Fork, not simply an old name for today's Southold hamlet. English settlement began in 1640, but the surviving record shows several transactions and later confirming deeds—not one uncontested purchase that transferred the entire Corchaug homeland at once.
activity_update_summary: Added a cited introduction explaining Yennicock's broad North Fork scope, Southold's 1640 settlement, the 1665 confirming deeds, Paucamp's 1660 testimony, and the layered nature of colonial land claims.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: Yennicock helps visitors see that a Native place-name could describe a landscape larger than a later town center. Reading the 1640 settlement, repeated deeds, and Paucamp's testimony together prevents the North Fork from being reduced to one colonial founding date. It also keeps Native geographic knowledge, Corchaug authority, and the uneven conversion of homeland into surveyed property visible.
introduction_title: Yennicock, Southold, and the North Fork
introduction_content: Yennicock and Yennicott are among the spellings preserved in seventeenth-century records for the North Fork. William Wallace Tooker interpreted the name as “at the extended land or country” and argued that records sometimes applied it broadly from the Peconic River to Plum Gut, not only to today's Southold hamlet. English settlers organized a New Haven colony settlement here in 1640, but the documentary trail is incomplete: Southold's earliest town records largely do not survive, and the remaining sources describe separate transactions involving different people and places. In 1665, settlers put earlier claims into writing through confirming deeds; this was not the first and only transfer. Paucamp's 1660 testimony also preserved Native knowledge of Peconic headwater boundaries, fishing places, and long-standing sachemship. Together, these records show a named Corchaug homeland being translated into colonial property over time—not one simple purchase followed by disappearance.
land_loss_title: Repeated deeds and colonial land claims
land_loss_content:
Southold's surviving record does not describe one complete, uncontested purchase. Town historian Amy Folk notes that some of the earliest local transactions were not written down when they occurred. In 1665, settlers created confirming deeds to put earlier claims into written form; the Southold deed included marks attributed to Corchaug men, including Ambusco and Paucamp. Other deeds and town actions concerned Hashamomuck, Aquebogue, Mattituck, Cutchogue, Oysterponds, Plum Island, Wading River, and Robins Island at different times.

These records show how colonial governments translated different Native relationships to land into English property claims. They document negotiation and pressure, but they should not be read as one transaction that completely described every Corchaug relationship to the North Fork.
